solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because Section 8 is indeed in the same Biological Diversity Act, 2002, but it governs the National Biodiversity Authority, not State Biodiversity Boards.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Section 8 establishes the National Biodiversity Authority, not the SBBs.
Eliminate (c): Section 37 deals with Biodiversity Heritage Sites, a distinct provision.
Eliminate (d): Section 41 governs Biodiversity Management Committees at the local body level.
Retain (b): Section 22 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 is the specific statutory basis for SBB establishment.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students who know that both NBA and SBBs are constituted under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 may confuse the section numbers. Section 8 (NBA) and Section 22 (SBBs) are both in the same Act, making (a) a tempting choice for those who recall 'Section 8' without remembering which tier it governs. The trap exploits the 'same Act, different section' design of the three-tier framework.
solution.final_explanation:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 creates a three-tier governance structure. While the National Biodiversity Authority is established under Section 8, State Biodiversity Boards find their statutory basis in Section 22 of the same Act. This parallelism is deliberate — the same legislative instrument creates all three tiers, but through distinct sections.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 8 establishes the National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), the apex body at the central level.
• Option (b) — Correct: Section 22 mandates the constitution of State Biodiversity Boards by state governments.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Section 37 empowers state governments to notify Biodiversity Heritage Sites.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Section 41 requires local bodies to constitute Biodiversity Management Committees.

Value Addition:
• The BD Act, 2002 has 65 sections and covers all three tiers in a single legislation.
• SBBs regulate Indian companies' access; NBA regulates foreign access — jurisdictional split by nationality.
• Section 22 makes SBB constitution mandatory for states, unlike some discretionary state environment bodies.

concepts_used: Regulatory Role of SBBs — Prior Intimation vs. Prior Approval

solution.concept_anchor: Section 7 — intimation not approval for Indian entities

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 7 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, Indian companies intending to access biological resources for commercial purposes must obtain prior approval from the State Biodiversity Board.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 7 requires only prior intimation to the SBB, not prior approval — a critical distinction that separates the domestic regime from the stricter foreign-entity regime under Section 3.

statement_analysis.statement: Foreign nationals and foreign-incorporated companies seeking access to India's biological resources are governed by Section 3 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, which requires approval from the National Biodiversity Authority.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 3 places foreign entities and non-resident Indians under NBA's prior approval requirement, clearly distinguishing this from the SBB intimation mechanism applicable to Indian citizens under Section 7.

statement_analysis.statement: Failure to intimate the State Biodiversity Board as required under Section 7 can attract penalties including imprisonment of up to three years under Section 55 of the Act.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 55 prescribes penalties for contraventions of Section 7, including imprisonment up to three years or a monetary fine or both, making non-intimation a cognizable offence.

solution.strong_distractor: b — A student who knows Statements 2 and 3 are correct may choose (b) without carefully checking Statement 1, assuming 'prior intimation' and 'prior approval' are interchangeable regulatory concepts.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: it uses the phrase 'prior approval' for Indian companies — Section 7 requires only 'prior intimation'; Statement 1 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 2: NBA approval for foreign entities under Section 3 is accurate; Statement 2 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: Section 55 penalties for Section 7 violations including three-year imprisonment are correct; Statement 3 is correct.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The prior intimation vs. prior approval distinction is one of the most frequently exploited traps in BD Act questions. 'Approval' implies a decision-making power that could block access, whereas 'intimation' merely requires notification. A student reading quickly equates both terms and marks Statement 1 as correct. This inflates the answer to (d) — all three correct — which violates the actual statutory design.
solution.final_explanation:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 creates differentiated access obligations based on who is seeking access. For foreign entities, Section 3 mandates prior approval from the NBA — access can be denied. For Indian citizens and companies, Section 7 requires only prior intimation to the SBB — access cannot be blocked by this mechanism alone, only regulated.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The word 'approval' makes this wrong. Section 7 uses 'intimation.' Indian entities notify but do not seek permission from SBBs.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Section 3 squarely places foreign nationals, NRIs, and foreign companies under NBA's prior approval regime.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Section 55 backs Section 7's intimation requirement with penal teeth — up to three years' imprisonment or fine or both.

Value Addition:
• The intimation-vs-approval gap reflects India's sovereign flexibility — Indian entities have lighter compliance burdens than foreign ones.
• NBA has additional power to compound offences; SBBs must approach courts.
• Section 61 ensures no court takes cognizance of offences except on complaint by NBA or SBB.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 7 proviso — exemptions from SBB intimation

statement_analysis.statement: The proviso to Section 7 exempts local communities accessing biological resources for personal, non-commercial use from the requirement to intimate the State Biodiversity Board.
statement_analysis.reason: The proviso to Section 7 explicitly exempts local communities, cultivators, and growers accessing biological resources for personal use from the SBB intimation requirement — this is a correctly stated exemption.

statement_analysis.statement: Vaids and Hakims practising indigenous medicine are exempted from approaching both the State Biodiversity Board and the National Biodiversity Authority under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002.
statement_analysis.reason: The exemption for Vaids and Hakims applies specifically to the SBB jurisdiction under Section 7 — they are not exempted from NBA requirements if their activity falls under Section 3; the exemption regimes are distinct for each tier.

statement_analysis.statement: The exemption granted to cultivators of biological resources under the Section 7 proviso extends to commercial cultivation for export purposes.
statement_analysis.reason: The proviso's exemption covers personal use and local subsistence activities — commercial cultivation, especially for export, would attract Section 7's intimation obligation and falls outside the exemption's scope.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Statement 1 alone being incorrect seems plausible to a student who misreads the proviso as covering commercial use as well; but Statement 1 is actually correct, making it an unreliable choice.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: personal use exemption for local communities under Section 7 proviso is accurately stated — Statement 1 is correct, not an incorrect statement.
Evaluate Statement 2: extending Vaid/Hakim exemption to NBA jurisdiction is factually wrong — the exemption is SBB-specific — Statement 2 is incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: commercial export cultivation is outside the personal-use exemption — Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 exploits students' tendency to extend an exemption across the entire Act rather than limiting it to the specific tier where it operates. Vaids and Hakims practising indigenous medicine receive relief from SBB intimation, but that exemption does not travel up to the NBA tier. A partially prepared student seeing 'Vaids and Hakims are exempt' in their notes marks Statement 2 as correct, failing to catch the 'both NBA and SBB' overreach.
solution.final_explanation:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 balances community rights with regulatory oversight through targeted exemptions in the proviso to Section 7. These exemptions are tier-specific and purpose-limited.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The proviso to Section 7 clearly shields local communities, cultivators, and growers accessing resources for personal use from the SBB intimation requirement.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The exemption for practitioners of indigenous medicine (Vaids, Hakims) is limited to SBB's jurisdiction. If their activities attract Section 3 obligations, NBA requirements apply separately. The two exemption regimes do not merge.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The exemption covers personal and subsistence use, not commercial cultivation for export. Commercial exploitation would trigger Section 7 obligations.

Value Addition:
• The 2023 Amendment additionally exempts AYUSH practitioners and codified traditional knowledge — expanding exemption coverage beyond the original proviso.
• Exemptions under the BD Act are consistent with CBD's principle of protecting community rights to traditional resources.
• The Forest Rights Act, 2006 independently governs Scheduled Tribes' traditional use and operates separately from BD Act exemptions.

solution.concept_anchor: Three-tier biodiversity governance — jurisdictional assignments

statement_analysis.statement: The National Biodiversity Authority regulates access by foreign nationals and foreign companies to India's biological resources.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 3 of the BD Act places foreign-entity access under NBA's prior approval — this is the NBA's core regulatory function and is correctly stated.

statement_analysis.statement: Biodiversity Management Committees are constituted directly under the supervision of the National Biodiversity Authority.
statement_analysis.reason: BMCs are constituted at the local body level under the guidance and oversight of State Biodiversity Boards — the SBB is the intermediary tier; NBA does not directly supervise BMCs.

statement_analysis.statement: State Biodiversity Boards regulate access to biological resources by Indian companies for commercial purposes through a prior intimation mechanism.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 7 assigns this regulatory role to SBBs with a prior intimation (not approval) requirement for Indian commercial entities — correctly described.

statement_analysis.statement: The People's Biodiversity Register is a national-level strategy document prepared by the National Biodiversity Authority to guide conservation planning.
statement_analysis.reason: PBR is a local-level documentation tool prepared by BMCs under SBB guidance — it records local biological resources and knowledge; the national strategy document is the NBSAP, prepared by MoEFCC/NBA.

solution.strong_distractor: c — A student who correctly identifies the NBA–foreign entity and SBB–Indian company roles may assume three statements are correct, overlooking that Statement 4 conflates PBR with NBSAP.
elimination_logic: Statement 1 is correct — NBA's Section 3 jurisdiction over foreign entities is a foundational BD Act provision.
Statement 2 is incorrect — BMCs are supervised by SBBs, not directly by NBA; the three-tier structure places SBB between NBA and BMC.
Statement 3 is correct — SBB's Section 7 prior intimation role for Indian commercial entities is accurately described.
Statement 4 is incorrect — PBR is a local documentation register prepared by BMCs, not a national strategy by NBA; that is the NBSAP.
Only two statements (1 and 3) are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the common misconception that the NBA, being the apex body, directly oversees all tiers including BMCs. The three-tier design deliberately places SBBs as the intermediary — BMCs report upward through SBBs. Statement 4 exploits the PBR–NBSAP confusion: both are biodiversity-related documents, but PBR is hyper-local while NBSAP is the national policy framework.
solution.final_explanation:
India's biodiversity governance is structured as NBA (national) → SBB (state) → BMC (local), with non-overlapping jurisdictions and a clear chain of supervision.

| Pair | Verdict |
|---|---|
| NBA regulates foreign entity access (Section 3) | Correct |
| BMCs directly supervised by NBA | Incorrect |
| SBBs regulate Indian commercial access (Section 7 intimation) | Correct |
| PBR is a national NBA document | Incorrect |

Only two statements are correct — option (b).

Value Addition:
• Fund flow mirrors the hierarchy: NBA national fund → SBBs → BMC-level conservation work.
• NBSAP (National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan) is the national planning instrument; PBR is a village-level documentation register.
• Section 41 of the BD Act mandates every local body to constitute a BMC — SBBs are the guiding authority for this.
• NBA reports to Parliament; SBBs report to State Legislatures — parallel but distinct accountability tracks.

solution.concept_anchor: SBB–NBA relationship — subordinate not hierarchically controlled
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may assume that the NBA's higher status automatically explains SBBs implementing NBA guidelines, missing that the causal link is statutory (Section 23(d)), not hierarchical control.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. Section 23(d) of the BD Act requires SBBs to take steps to implement guidelines issued by the NBA.
Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. SBBs report to State Legislatures while the NBA reports to Parliament — these are parallel but distinct accountability tracks established under the Act.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — No. SBBs implement NBA guidelines because Section 23(d) statutorily mandates it, not because of their separate accountability tracks. The parallel reporting structures are a consequence of the federal design, not the cause of guideline-implementation obligations.
Both A and R are correct but R does NOT explain A — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is the plausibility of R as an explanation for A. Students who know both facts — that SBBs implement NBA guidelines and that they have separate reporting tracks — may hastily conclude that the reporting hierarchy explains the implementation obligation. In fact, Section 23(d) is a direct statutory command, independent of reporting structures. The two accountability tracks (Parliament vs. State Legislature) reflect federal design, not causal logic for guideline implementation.
solution.final_explanation:
The BD Act creates a federal biodiversity governance architecture where the NBA and SBBs have parallel statutory foundations but distinct accountability tracks.

Assertion (A): Correct. Section 23(d) of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 explicitly requires SBBs to take steps to implement guidelines issued by the National Biodiversity Authority. This is a direct statutory mandate.

Reason (R): Correct. SBBs submit annual reports to State Legislatures, while the NBA reports to Parliament. This reflects the federal division of the Act across Union-state lines and is an independently verifiable fact.

Causal Link: R does not explain A. SBBs implement NBA guidelines because Section 23(d) commands it — not because their accountability tracks differ. The separate reporting structures reflect constitutional federalism, while the implementation obligation is a product of the three-tier design. These are parallel facts without a causal connection.

Correct option: (c) — A correct, R correct, R does NOT explain A.

Value Addition:
• No formal joint inspection or monitoring mechanism between NBA and SBBs is prescribed in the BD Act — an acknowledged implementation gap.
• ABS proceeds flow from NBA's national fund partially to SBBs, linking them financially despite separate accountability.
• The 2023 Amendment altered some compliance burdens but did not change the Section 23(d) guideline-implementation mandate.

solution.concept_anchor: Nagoya Protocol timeline — adoption, ratification by India
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know India ratified the Nagoya Protocol 'around 2012' but confuse the Protocol's adoption year (2010) with its entry into force date (2014) will choose option (a) placing ratification before entry into force incorrectly.
elimination_logic: The Convention on Biological Diversity was adopted at Rio Earth Summit in 1992 — this is the earliest event.
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 was enacted domestically — comes after CBD 1992.
The Nagoya Protocol was adopted at COP10 in Nagoya in 2010 — after BD Act 2002.
India ratified the Nagoya Protocol in 2012 — after its adoption in 2010 but before its global entry into force in 2014.
Correct sequence: CBD 1992 → BD Act 2002 → Nagoya Protocol adoption 2010 → India's ratification 2012 → Nagoya Protocol entry into force 2014 — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Nagoya Protocol timeline is a fertile trap zone. Students confuse adoption (2010), India's ratification (2012), and global entry into force (2014). Many students know India ratified 'before' the Protocol entered into force but may place the BD Act after the Nagoya Protocol, reversing the domestic-international sequencing. Additionally, the CBD's 1992 date is sometimes confused with its entry into force in 1993.
solution.final_explanation:
Understanding the chronological layering of biodiversity law — from international conventions to domestic legislation to protocol ratifications — is essential for SBB-related questions.

Correct sequence: CBD adoption (1992) → Biological Diversity Act (2002) → Nagoya Protocol adopted at COP10 (2010) → India ratifies Nagoya Protocol (2012) → Nagoya Protocol enters into force globally (2014).

• Option (a) incorrectly positions India's ratification after global entry into force — India ratified in 2012, two years before the Protocol came into force internationally in 2014.
• Option (b) is correct: the sequence respects all dates accurately.
• Option (c) places the Nagoya Protocol before the BD Act — this reverses the domestic-international sequence; the BD Act 2002 predates the Protocol by eight years.
• Option (d) places CBD after the BD Act — impossible, as the CBD (1992) is the parent obligation that prompted the BD Act (2002).

Value Addition:
• The Nagoya Protocol has 138 parties as of 2024; it operationalizes the ABS pillar of the CBD.
• India's 2012 ratification strengthens SBBs' role as domestic checkpoint authorities for ABS compliance.
• The Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (2022) sets the 30×30 area conservation target — a new reference for SBB area-based work.

solution.concept_anchor: PBR vs NBSAP — different instruments different levels
solution.strong_distractor: b — The National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan sounds like it could be a local documentation tool alongside PBR because both deal with biodiversity; students unfamiliar with NBSAP's national-level formulation may not identify it as the odd one out.
elimination_logic: Identify the common attribute: which three items are local/community-level biodiversity documentation or planning instruments under SBB/BMC framework?
People's Biodiversity Register — prepared by BMCs, records local biological resources and practices — local instrument.
Traditional Knowledge Digital Library — records traditional knowledge for defensive publication to prevent biopiracy — national instrument but complementary to local documentation.
Village-level conservation plans under BMC guidance — local planning documents under SBB oversight.
National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan — prepared by MoEFCC/NBA as the national policy framework — NOT a local or SBB-level instrument.
NBSAP is the odd one out — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: NBSAP and PBR both deal with biodiversity documentation, making them appear similar to a student scanning options quickly. The distinction is hierarchical: PBR is a village-level register prepared by BMCs under SBB oversight, while NBSAP is a national-level strategic plan formulated by MoEFCC and the NBA. TKDL, though national in scope, is a defensive publication tool complementary to local documentation — it does not belong to SBB's instruments either, but the question tests the most obvious odd-one-out in the context of community-level mechanisms.
solution.final_explanation:
The question tests whether students can distinguish between biodiversity instruments operating at different governance tiers.

• Option (a) — People's Biodiversity Register: Prepared by Biodiversity Management Committees under SBB guidance — a local-level documentation tool recording biological resources, traditional knowledge, and practices. Belongs to the SBB/BMC framework.
• Option (b) — Traditional Knowledge Digital Library: A national repository managed by CSIR that records traditional medicinal knowledge for defensive publication against biopiracy. While national in scope, it complements local documentation and is frequently discussed alongside PBR in SBB contexts.
• Option (c) — BMC Conservation Plan: Village-level or panchayat-level conservation planning under SBB guidance — firmly in the local governance tier.
• Option (d) — National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP): Formulated by MoEFCC in coordination with NBA as India's national biodiversity policy framework. It is NOT prepared by SBBs — SBBs implement national strategy, not formulate it.

NBSAP is the odd one out — it is a national planning document, not a local documentation or SBB-level instrument.

Value Addition:
• India's updated NBSAP was submitted to CBD in 2023 ahead of the Kunming-Montreal targets.
• PBRs have evidentiary value in IPR disputes and ABS negotiations.
• TKDL is under CSIR/DIPP, not SBB — but SBBs can use TKDL data to strengthen biopiracy prevention.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 61 — cognizance of offences, SBB enforcement limits

statement_analysis.statement: Under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, no court shall take cognizance of an offence under the Act except upon a complaint made by the National Biodiversity Authority or a State Biodiversity Board.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 61 of the BD Act contains exactly this safeguard — courts cannot suo motu take cognizance; they must wait for a formal complaint from either NBA or an SBB, giving these bodies gate-keeping power over prosecutions.

statement_analysis.statement: State Biodiversity Boards possess independent authority to compound offences under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, similar to the powers vested in the National Biodiversity Authority.
statement_analysis.reason: The power to compound offences is vested in the NBA — SBBs must approach the State Government or courts to enforce penalties; they do not have independent compounding authority equivalent to the NBA's.

solution.strong_distractor: a — A student who knows Section 61's complaint mechanism and wrongly assumes SBBs and NBA have symmetric enforcement powers will mark both statements correct and choose (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 61 of the BD Act restricts court cognizance to complaints by NBA or SBBs — this is a precisely accurate statutory provision; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: the power to compound offences belongs to NBA, not SBBs — SBBs have limited enforcement and must route actions through courts or State Government; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 is the assumption of symmetry — students who know NBA can compound offences may assume SBBs have the same power because the penalty provisions appear parallel. In practice, SBBs lack independent compounding authority, which is a significant asymmetry in the enforcement architecture. This asymmetry reflects the weaker institutional capacity designed for state-level bodies relative to the apex national authority.
solution.final_explanation:
The Biological Diversity Act's enforcement provisions are asymmetric between the NBA and SBBs, a distinction that UPSC frequently probes.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 61 is a clear safeguard — courts require a formal complaint from either NBA or an SBB before taking cognizance of any offence under the Act. This prevents frivolous litigation and gives biodiversity bodies prosecutorial control.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Compounding of offences is a power reserved for the NBA. SBBs must approach courts (Section 56 for civil remedies, Section 55 for criminal penalties) or the State Government — they cannot independently compound (settle) violations the way NBA can.

Value Addition:
• Section 56 provides SBBs access to civil court injunctions against biopiracy.
• The asymmetry in compounding powers reflects the NBA's status as a statutory authority with quasi-judicial functions.
• CAG reports have cited SBBs' inability to independently enforce as a structural weakness in biodiversity governance.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students may confuse Section 32 (State Biodiversity Fund) with Section 27 (National Biodiversity Fund under NBA) because both funds have similar purposes, making option (d) tempting.

The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 establishes parallel fund structures at national and state levels. The National Biodiversity Fund (Section 27) is managed by the NBA, while the State Biodiversity Fund is established under Section 32 and managed by SBBs.

• Option (c) — Incorrect: Section 37 governs Biodiversity Heritage Site notification by State Governments.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Section 27 governs the National Biodiversity Fund at the central level under NBA.

Value Addition:

• CAG oversight applies to both National and State Biodiversity Funds.
• The two-fund parallel structure mirrors the NBA–SBB two-tier regulatory architecture.

solution.final_explanation:
Biopiracy prevention involves multiple institutional mechanisms, and students must precisely attribute each mechanism to its correct managing authority.

• Option (a) — Correctly matched: Section 56 of the BD Act provides civil remedy access — SBBs can approach courts for injunctions against unauthorized access to biological resources within state territory.

statement_analysis.statement: The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 exempts practitioners of Ayurveda, Yoga, Unani, Siddha, and Homeopathy (AYUSH) from the prior intimation requirement to State Biodiversity Boards when accessing biological resources for their practice.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2023 Amendment specifically exempts AYUSH practitioners from provisions of the BD Act that would require SBB intimation, reducing the regulatory burden on traditional medicine practitioners.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2023 Amendment to the Biological Diversity Act removed the requirement for Indian researchers to seek prior approval from the National Biodiversity Authority before conducting research on biological resources.
statement_analysis.reason: Indian researchers were already not required to seek NBA approval — they needed only SBB intimation. The 2023 Amendment relaxed the prior intimation requirement for certain categories of Indian researchers, but it did not 'remove NBA approval requirements' which were never applicable to Indian researchers in the first place.

statement_analysis.statement: Critics of the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 argue that exempting codified traditional knowledge from BD Act provisions weakens the Access and Benefit Sharing regime and reduces State Biodiversity Boards' ability to monitor commercial exploitation.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the documented criticism from biodiversity experts and tribal groups — that exempting codified traditional knowledge removes it from the ABS regulatory oversight of SBBs, potentially enabling commercial exploitation without community benefit sharing.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who support all three statements as true — especially those who confuse 'NBA approval' with 'SBB intimation' for Indian researchers — will mark Statement 2 correct and choose (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: AYUSH practitioner exemption under 2023 Amendment is an accurately stated policy change — correct.

Evaluate Statement 2: Indian researchers never needed NBA prior approval — they needed SBB intimation. The statement incorrectly frames the reform as removing an NBA requirement that never existed for Indian researchers — incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: The codified traditional knowledge exemption criticism is accurately described and well-documented in parliamentary debates — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits the NBA-vs-SBB jurisdictional confusion. Students who know the 2023 Amendment relaxed research requirements may assume this involved NBA prior approval — but Indian researchers were never subject to NBA approval. The reform relaxed SBB intimation requirements for certain Indian researchers. Framing the change as 'removing NBA approval' misleads students who have not precisely mapped the pre-amendment compliance framework.
solution.final_explanation:
The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 significantly altered the compliance landscape, with direct implications for SBBs' regulatory role.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The 2023 Amendment exempts AYUSH practitioners from BD Act provisions, reducing SBBs' oversight over one of the largest traditional-medicine user categories.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Indian researchers were never subject to NBA prior approval — that requirement applies only to foreign entities under Section 3. The 2023 Amendment relaxed SBB intimation (not NBA approval) obligations for Indian researchers. The framing 'removed NBA approval requirement' is factually wrong.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Exempting codified traditional knowledge from ABS provisions is the central critique from biodiversity experts and tribal communities — SBBs lose monitoring authority over commercially valuable traditional knowledge once it is classified as 'codified.'

• The seed sector was also exempted, raising concerns about corporate access to agro-biodiversity without ABS obligations.

solution.concept_anchor: SBB jurisdiction ends at territorial waters — marine biodiversity
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may assume that the EEZ boundary naturally explains SBB's jurisdictional limit — but the causal explanation for territorial limits is the BD Act's jurisdictional design, not the EEZ definition alone.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. SBBs of coastal states have jurisdiction over marine biological resources within territorial waters; beyond territorial waters, into the Exclusive Economic Zone and beyond, the Central Government and NBA act — this jurisdictional limit is correct.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — No. The Reason states SBBs have no role in agro-biodiversity conservation — this is factually incorrect. The BD Act mandates SBBs to conserve agro-biodiversity and landraces, and they interface with the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 in this regard.
Step 3: Moot — since R is incorrect, the answer is (c): A correct, R incorrect.
Select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Reason is carefully crafted to sound authoritative — 'SBBs' mandate is limited to wild species conservation' is a plausible-sounding but incorrect claim. The BD Act explicitly covers biological resources broadly, including agro-biodiversity and cultivated varieties. Students who associate biodiversity conservation only with wild species (influenced by the Wildlife Protection Act's Schedule-based approach) may accept R without scrutiny.
solution.final_explanation:
The BD Act's scope is deliberately broader than species-centric conservation laws like the Wildlife Protection Act.

Assertion (A): Correct. SBB jurisdiction in marine areas is limited to territorial waters (12 nautical miles). Beyond that, including the Exclusive Economic Zone (200 nautical miles), the Central Government and NBA exercise authority. This jurisdictional boundary is an important marine biodiversity governance point.

Reason (R): Incorrect. The claim that SBBs have no role in agro-biodiversity conservation is factually wrong. The BD Act's mandate to SBBs explicitly includes biological resources broadly — covering agricultural biodiversity, landraces, and crop wild relatives. SBBs interface with the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 on agro-biodiversity issues.

Since A is correct but R is incorrect, the answer is (c).

Value Addition:
• The PPV&FR Act, 2001 protects farmers' rights over plant varieties and interfaces with the BD Act's agro-biodiversity conservation mandate.
• India's territorial sea extends 12 nautical miles; contiguous zone up to 24 NM; EEZ up to 200 NM from baseline.
• The Kunming-Montreal 30×30 target includes marine areas — increasing relevance of coastal SBBs' documentation role.

solution.concept_anchor: SBB implementation gaps — BMC constitution rate, staffing

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary Standing Committee and Comptroller and Auditor General reports have highlighted that most State Biodiversity Boards across India are either non-functional or severely under-resourced.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an accurately documented finding — CAG and Parliamentary Standing Committee reports have consistently flagged inadequate staffing, funding, and technical capacity as primary reasons for SBB dysfunction.

statement_analysis.statement: The low rate of Biodiversity Management Committee constitution across states is primarily attributable to a legal ambiguity in Section 41 of the BD Act, which leaves BMC formation to the discretion of local bodies.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 41 does not leave BMC formation to discretion — it mandates every local body to constitute a BMC. The low constitution rate reflects practical implementation failures (awareness gaps, resource constraints, SBB capacity), not a legal ambiguity in the section itself.

statement_analysis.statement: The Indian Biodiversity Portal serves as the central digital repository for all State Biodiversity Fund transactions, enabling real-time public audit of SBB financial flows.
statement_analysis.reason: The Indian Biodiversity Portal is a citizen science platform for biological observations — it is not a financial audit mechanism for SBB fund transactions. No real-time public audit system for State Biodiversity Fund flows exists under the BD Act framework.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Statement 1 being true means it is NOT in the 'incorrect' category — students who read carelessly and see 'CAG + SBBs non-functional' as a correct-sounding claim may include it as an incorrect statement.
elimination_logic: The question asks which statements are NOT correct — identify the false statements.
Statement 1: CAG and Parliamentary Standing Committee findings on SBB dysfunction are accurately stated — Statement 1 is correct (not an incorrect statement).
Statement 2: Section 41 mandates BMC formation — it is not discretionary. Attributing low constitution rate to 'legal ambiguity' is a fabricated explanation — Statement 2 is NOT correct.
Statement 3: Indian Biodiversity Portal is a species-observation platform, not a financial audit system — the claim about real-time SBB fund audit is fabricated — Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a plausible-fabrication trap. 'Indian Biodiversity Portal' is a real platform, making the statement sound authoritative. A student who associates the portal with the BD Act ecosystem may not scrutinize its actual function. The claim about 'real-time public audit' of SBB fund flows is entirely fabricated — no such mechanism exists. Statement 2 exploits students' assumption that legal ambiguity always underlies implementation failures, when in this case Section 41 is unambiguous and the failure is purely administrative.
solution.final_explanation:
The implementation gap in India's biodiversity governance is well-documented but requires precise attribution of causes.

• Statement 1 — Correct: CAG reports and Parliamentary Standing Committee reviews have consistently flagged SBB dysfunction — this is accurately stated and not an incorrect statement.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: Section 41 is unambiguous — it mandates every local body to constitute a BMC. The low constitution rate stems from administrative failures, awareness gaps, and SBB capacity constraints, not from statutory ambiguity.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: The Indian Biodiversity Portal is a citizen science platform for recording biological observations — it has no role as a financial audit system for SBB fund transactions. The claim is fabricated.

Value Addition:
• As of recent CAG reports, several states have negligible BMC constitution rates despite Section 41's mandatory language.
• Lack of awareness among Indian companies about Section 7 intimation requirements is a documented regulatory gap cited in governance reviews.
• The 2023 Amendment reduced some compliance obligations but did not address SBBs' fundamental resource and capacity deficits.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know SBBs are involved in biodiversity strategy implementation may confuse 'implementation' with 'formulation' and attribute NBSAP preparation to SBBs.
elimination_logic: The question asks which body prepares India's National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan.
Eliminate (a): Local bodies prepare People's Biodiversity Registers — not national strategy documents.
Eliminate (b): SBBs implement national biodiversity strategy — they do not formulate or prepare the NBSAP.
Eliminate (c): BMCs prepare People's Biodiversity Registers at the local level.
Select (d): The NBSAP is prepared by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change in coordination with the National Biodiversity Authority — not by SBBs.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The formulation-vs-implementation distinction is the trap here. SBBs are active implementers of biodiversity strategy at the state level, which leads students to associate them with strategic planning. The NBSAP, however, is prepared by MoEFCC in coordination with the NBA — a national-level exercise. SBBs contribute data and local insights but do not formulate the national strategy document.
solution.final_explanation:
India's National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan (NBSAP) is the country's primary national commitment document under the Convention on Biological Diversity.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Local bodies are responsible for People's Biodiversity Register preparation — not national strategy documents.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: SBBs are implementation bodies. Section 23(d) requires them to implement NBA guidelines — they are not the formulating authority for national strategy.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: BMCs prepare PBRs at the local level; they have no role in national planning documents.
• Option (d) — Correct: India's NBSAP is prepared by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) in coordination with the National Biodiversity Authority. India submitted an updated NBSAP in 2023 ahead of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework targets.

Value Addition:

• NBSAP is submitted to the CBD Secretariat — it is India's international commitment document.
• SBBs contribute state-level data to NBSAP but do not formulate it — a distinction critical for UPSC answer-writing.

solution.concept_anchor: SBB vs Forest Rights Act — Scheduled Tribes traditional use

statement_analysis.statement: State Biodiversity Boards have no regulatory authority over the traditional use of biological resources by Scheduled Tribes, as such use is independently governed by the Forest Rights Act, 2006.
statement_analysis.reason: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 operates independently of the BD Act — SBBs cannot override or regulate the rights recognized for Scheduled Tribes under the FRA; these are parallel legislative regimes.

statement_analysis.statement: State Biodiversity Boards and State Pollution Control Boards have a formally prescribed coordination mechanism under the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 to prevent duplication of environmental regulatory oversight.
statement_analysis.reason: No formal coordination mechanism between SBBs and State Pollution Control Boards is prescribed in the BD Act — this is an acknowledged implementation gap where two bodies with overlapping environmental mandates operate without statutory coordination requirements.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly know Statement 1 is true may assume the BD Act must have some inter-board coordination mechanism and mark Statement 2 as true too, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The Forest Rights Act, 2006 operates independently and protects Scheduled Tribes' traditional use beyond SBB jurisdiction — correctly stated; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: No formal coordination mechanism between SBBs and SPCBs exists in the BD Act — this gap is well-documented; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 sounds procedurally reasonable — two environmental bodies sharing mandates should logically coordinate. Students assume that since both SBBs and State Pollution Control Boards operate in the environmental domain, the BD Act must have prescribed a coordination mechanism. In reality, this is an explicit governance gap — no such mechanism is prescribed, and the two bodies operate in silos. This institutional fragmentation is a recurring criticism in environmental governance literature.
solution.final_explanation:
SBBs operate within a complex web of state-level bodies with partially overlapping environmental mandates.

• Statement 1 — Correct: SBBs have no regulatory authority over Scheduled Tribes' traditional use of biological resources. The Forest Rights Act, 2006 independently recognizes and protects these rights. The two Acts operate as parallel regimes — SBB authority does not override FRA protections.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The BD Act prescribes no formal coordination mechanism between SBBs and State Pollution Control Boards. Despite shared environmental concerns — SBBs on biological diversity, SPCBs on pollution — they function in institutional silos. This fragmentation is cited as a governance gap in multiple administrative reviews.

Value Addition:
• SBB vs. State Forest Department overlap on NTFPs (Non-Timber Forest Produce) is another documented jurisdictional conflict without statutory resolution.
• A single biodiversity-rich area could theoretically fall under SBB (BD Act), Forest Department (Forest Act), and SPCB (Environment Protection Act) jurisdiction simultaneously.
• The 2023 Amendment did not address these inter-institutional coordination gaps.

solution.concept_anchor: ABS — NBA finalizes foreign agreements, SBB oversees domestic commercial

statement_analysis.statement: The National Biodiversity Authority finalizes Access and Benefit Sharing agreements with foreign entities seeking access to India's biological resources, while State Biodiversity Boards oversee ABS arrangements for domestic commercial use by Indian companies.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately captures the jurisdictional split: NBA handles foreign ABS (Section 3), SBBs handle domestic commercial ABS (Section 7) — a fundamental design principle of the BD Act.

statement_analysis.statement: India ratified the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit Sharing in 2014, when the Protocol also entered into force globally.
statement_analysis.reason: India ratified the Nagoya Protocol in 2012 — two years before the Protocol entered into force globally in 2014. Conflating India's ratification date with the global entry-into-force date is the targeted trap.

statement_analysis.statement: Proceeds from Access and Benefit Sharing agreements involving foreign entities are received by the National Biodiversity Authority and a portion is channeled to State Biodiversity Boards for state-level conservation activities.
statement_analysis.reason: The fund flow mechanism under the BD Act runs from NBA's national fund to SBBs — ABS proceeds at the national level partially support state-level conservation through SBBs, linking the two tiers financially.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know all three topics are broadly accurate may not catch the 2012-vs-2014 confusion in Statement 2, marking all three correct and choosing (d).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: NBA-foreign entity ABS vs. SBB-domestic commercial ABS split is accurately described — correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: India ratified Nagoya Protocol in 2012; the Protocol entered into force globally in 2014 — conflating the two dates makes Statement 2 incorrect.
Evaluate Statement 3: Fund flow from NBA to SBBs for ABS proceeds is an accurately described financial linkage — correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a classic temporal trap — both years (2012 and 2014) are associated with the Nagoya Protocol. Students who remember 'India and Nagoya Protocol — 2014' without distinguishing ratification from entry into force will mark Statement 2 correct. The two years are close enough to be confused but are legally distinct events.
solution.final_explanation:
The Nagoya Protocol's timeline and the NBA-SBB ABS jurisdictional split are two high-frequency UPSC themes that intersect in this question.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The ABS architecture is split by the entity-type: NBA handles foreign entity agreements, SBBs oversee domestic commercial use. This prevents conflation of regulatory roles.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India ratified the Nagoya Protocol in 2012; the Protocol entered into force globally in October 2014. These are distinct events. India was among the early ratifiers, ratifying before the Protocol's global entry into force.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Financial flows mirror the governance hierarchy. ABS proceeds at the national level feed into NBA's national fund, which partially channels funds to SBBs to support state-level conservation and community benefit-sharing programs.

Value Addition:
• The Nagoya Protocol was adopted at CBD COP10 in Nagoya, Japan, in 2010 — three distinct years: 2010 (adoption), 2012 (India ratification), 2014 (global entry into force).
• The Nagoya Protocol requires Parties to designate 'checkpoints' — SBBs function as domestic checkpoint authorities for compliance verification.
• India's ABS regime was strengthened post-Nagoya ratification but implementation at SBB level remains uneven.

Students may assume Central Government prescription extends to SBB composition. In fact, SBB composition details including member ratios are determined by State Governments under Section 22, preserving federal autonomy in SBB design.
solution.final_explanation:

solution.concept_anchor: Section 23(c) SBB advisory role to state government
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know SBBs have advisory functions may attribute this to Section 22 (SBB establishment) without knowing the specific advisory powers are listed in Section 23.
elimination_logic: The blank concerns the Section that specifically gives SBBs advisory powers to state governments on biodiversity conservation including EIA processes.
Eliminate (a): Section 22 establishes SBBs — it is the constitution provision, not the powers provision.
Eliminate (b): Section 32 establishes the State Biodiversity Fund.
Eliminate (d): Section 41 governs Biodiversity Management Committees.
Select (c): Section 23 enumerates the functions of SBBs, with Section 23(c) specifically covering the advisory role to state governments on biodiversity conservation matters including EIA.
solution.final_explanation:
The Biological Diversity Act, 2002 separates SBB constitution (Section 22) from SBB functions (Section 23). Students must know that powers and functions are enumerated in Section 23, not Section 22.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 22 establishes SBBs but does not enumerate their specific functions — it is the enabling provision for constitution.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Section 32 deals with the State Biodiversity Fund — a financial provision, not a powers provision.
• Option (c) — Correct: Section 23 lists SBB functions; Section 23(c) specifically grants advisory authority to advise state governments on biodiversity conservation matters, including providing recommendations during EIA processes for biodiversity-rich areas.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Section 41 mandates local bodies to constitute BMCs — a local governance provision.

Value Addition:

• SBBs' advisory role in EIA is non-binding — a recurring governance criticism in environmental impact assessment reform discussions.
• Biodiversity Impact Assessment (BIA) as a distinct tool is being advocated to give SBBs stronger formal input into development approvals.

solution.concept_anchor: SBB civil remedy — Section 56 court injunction against biopiracy
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know SBBs have enforcement functions may assume SBBs can directly cancel patents through NBA — confusing the domestic enforcement remedy (court injunction via Section 56) with an international patent cancellation mechanism.
elimination_logic: Scenario: A foreign company patents a plant compound derived from a species documented in a state's PBR without ABS compliance.
Identify the correct SBB remedy: Section 56 provides SBBs access to civil courts for injunctions against unauthorized access to biological resources.
Eliminate (a): SBBs cannot directly compel patent offices — patent cancellation requires legal challenge through courts, not direct SBB administrative action.
Eliminate (b): SBBs approach courts — they do not 'direct' NBA to cancel patents; NBA and SBBs have parallel functions, SBBs do not command NBA.
Eliminate (c): TKDL is managed by CSIR, not SBBs — SBBs cannot 'submit TKDL evidence' as an institutional action; they can use PBR documentation in court proceedings.

Select (d): The SBB's most appropriate legal remedy is to approach a competent court under Section 56 for an injunction against the foreign company's unauthorized use, using PBR documentation as evidentiary support.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the strong distractor — students who know NBA has ABS jurisdiction over foreign entities may assume SBBs route all foreign-entity actions through NBA, including patent cancellation. In reality, SBBs have their own direct access to courts under Section 56 for civil remedies — they do not need to 'direct' NBA. The scenario tests whether students know SBBs have independent legal standing to approach courts, separate from NBA's ABS enforcement powers.
solution.final_explanation:
When unauthorized commercial exploitation of biological resources occurs, the BD Act provides SBBs with a specific civil remedy mechanism.

In the scenario, a foreign company has patented a plant compound without fulfilling ABS obligations, and the resource is documented in the state's PBR. The SBB must identify its most legally appropriate remedy.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: SBBs cannot directly order patent offices to cancel patents — patent challenge is a judicial function requiring court proceedings, not direct administrative intervention by SBBs.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: SBBs do not 'direct' the NBA — the two bodies operate at separate tiers with distinct mandates. SBBs cannot issue commands to NBA; they may coordinate but not command.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: TKDL is managed by CSIR, not SBBs. While SBBs can use PBR documentation as evidence, they cannot institutionally 'submit TKDL evidence' — that is a CSIR function in patent opposition proceedings.
• Option (d) — Correct: Section 56 of the BD Act empowers SBBs to approach competent civil courts for injunctions restraining unauthorized access to biological resources. PBR documentation provides the evidentiary basis for demonstrating prior knowledge and community rights.

Value Addition:
• Section 56 civil remedy complements Section 55's criminal penalties — dual enforcement tracks.
• PBRs have been used in ABS negotiations to establish community priority rights — their evidentiary value is legally recognized.
• India's patent challenge in the Turmeric case was led through the US Patent Office by CSIR, not SBBs — institutional attribution matters.

solution.concept_anchor: BMCs — both Gram Panchayat and urban local bodies, Section 41

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 41 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, both rural local bodies (Gram Panchayats) and urban local bodies are mandated to constitute Biodiversity Management Committees.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 41 applies to all local bodies — rural and urban — not just Gram Panchayats. This is a scope extension trap because students often associate BMCs exclusively with rural/panchayat settings.

statement_analysis.statement: The primary function of a Biodiversity Management Committee is to prepare and maintain the People's Biodiversity Register, and the State Biodiversity Board is responsible for standardizing PBR formats and training BMC members.
statement_analysis.reason: PBR preparation is the BMC's primary function under the BD Act, and SBBs have a well-documented oversight role in standardizing formats and providing capacity training to BMC members.

statement_analysis.statement: The National Biodiversity Authority directly supervises the constitution and functioning of Biodiversity Management Committees, bypassing the State Biodiversity Board tier.
statement_analysis.reason: BMCs are supervised through SBBs — the three-tier structure places SBBs as the intermediary between NBA and BMCs. NBA does not directly supervise BMCs; this is a foundational principle of the tiered governance design.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Students who know all three topics are biodiversity-related may assume all three statements are correct without catching Statement 3's NBA-bypasses-SBB error.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 41 covers both Gram Panchayats and urban local bodies for BMC constitution — correctly stated; correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: PBR preparation as BMC's primary function with SBB standardization and training oversight — accurately described; correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: NBA directly supervising BMCs bypassing SBBs contradicts the three-tier structure — the SBB is the intermediary tier; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statements 1 and 2 correct, Statement 3 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 exploits the apex-body logic: students assume the NBA, as the supreme biodiversity authority, must have direct oversight over all lower tiers. The deliberate three-tier design insulates BMCs from direct NBA supervision, routing oversight through SBBs. This preserves the federal architecture and gives state-level bodies a meaningful role. The 'bypassing' formulation in Statement 3 is the precise distortion of the governance design.
solution.final_explanation:
The BMC tier is the most grassroots element of India's biodiversity governance, and understanding its correct supervisory relationships is essential.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 41 is not limited to Gram Panchayats — it mandates all local bodies, urban and rural, to constitute BMCs. Urban BMCs document biodiversity in urban green spaces, water bodies, and peri-urban areas.
• Statement 2 — Correct: PBR preparation is the core BMC function. SBBs provide PBR format standardization, training programs, and periodic review — maintaining quality control across thousands of BMCs in a state.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The NBA does not directly supervise BMCs. The three-tier structure is NBA (national policy and foreign ABS) → SBB (state oversight and domestic ABS) → BMC (local documentation). SBBs are the mandatory intermediary tier.

Value Addition:
• As of recent data, India has over 200,000 BMCs mandated but many states report dramatically lower actual constitution numbers.
• PBRs have legal standing in ABS negotiations and IPR disputes — making their quality an SBB responsibility.
• Urban BMCs' mandate to document city biodiversity is increasingly relevant given rapid urbanization and biodiversity loss in urban areas.

solution.concept_anchor: CBD objectives, Nagoya Protocol, Kunming-Montreal — SBB implementation roles
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who conflate Nagoya Protocol with the CBD's third objective will match A-3 instead of A-2, disrupting the entire matching sequence.
elimination_logic: Match A (Convention on Biological Diversity, 1992): CBD's three objectives are conservation, sustainable use, and equitable ABS — the third objective (ABS) is what SBBs operationalize at state level — matches with 2.
Match B (Nagoya Protocol, 2010): This specifically operationalizes the ABS pillar of the CBD; SBBs function as domestic checkpoint authorities for Nagoya compliance — matches with 4.
Match C (Kunming-Montreal GBF, 2022): The 30×30 target for area-based conservation by 2030 — SBBs' role in area conservation within state territory — matches with 1.
Match D (NBSAP): National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan — prepared by MoEFCC/NBA; SBBs implement, not formulate it — matches with 3.
Correct combination: A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3 — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Nagoya Protocol–CBD conflation is the primary trap. The Nagoya Protocol operationalizes the ABS pillar of the CBD, so students may confuse Nagoya (B) with CBD's ABS objective (A). Additionally, students unfamiliar with the Kunming-Montreal GBF (2022) may misplace the 30×30 target. NBSAP being formulated by MoEFCC/NBA (not SBBs) is the third precision point that students with 'SBBs implement strategy' knowledge may not recall in sufficient detail.
solution.final_explanation:
International biodiversity obligations and SBBs' domestic implementation roles form a critical intersection for UPSC preparation.

Correct Matches:
• A (CBD, 1992) → 2 (Three objectives: conservation, sustainable use, ABS — SBBs operationalize the third): The CBD's Access and Benefit Sharing objective is the foundational international mandate that SBBs implement domestically for state-level resources.
• B (Nagoya Protocol, 2010) → 4 (SBBs as domestic checkpoint authorities for ABS compliance): The Nagoya Protocol requires Parties to designate checkpoints; SBBs function as India's state-level checkpoint authorities verifying ABS compliance.
• C (Kunming-Montreal GBF, 2022) → 1 (30×30 area conservation target — SBBs' role in state-level area-based conservation): The 30×30 target requires 30% of land and oceans protected by 2030 — SBBs' BHS notification and documentation functions contribute to this target.
• D (NBSAP) → 3 (Prepared by MoEFCC/NBA; SBBs implement, not formulate): The NBSAP is a MoEFCC-NBA product — SBBs implement national strategy at state level but do not author it.

Trap: A and B both involve ABS — the distinction is that CBD established the objective while Nagoya operationalized it into binding checkpoint obligations.

Value Addition:
• India ratified Nagoya Protocol in 2012; it entered into force globally in 2014.
• The Kunming-Montreal GBF was adopted at CBD COP15 in December 2022 in Montreal.
• NBSAP is India's commitment document to CBD — updated in 2023 to align with Kunming-Montreal targets.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 55 — penalty quantum for Section 7 violation
solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who recall 'five years' imprisonment for environmental offences from other Acts like the Environment Protection Act, 1986 may select (c), applying knowledge from the wrong statute.
elimination_logic: The question asks the maximum imprisonment prescribed under Section 55 for violation of Section 7 (failure to intimate SBB).
Eliminate (a): One year is too low — Section 55's penalty reflects the seriousness of commercial biodiversity access violations.
Eliminate (c): Five years imprisonment is the penalty under other environmental statutes like the Environment Protection Act — not the BD Act's Section 55.
Eliminate (d): Ten years is not prescribed anywhere in the BD Act.
Select (b): Section 55 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 prescribes imprisonment up to three years, or a monetary fine, or both for contravening Section 7.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits cross-statute penalty confusion. Students preparing across multiple environmental laws (EPA 1986, Wildlife Protection Act, BD Act) sometimes apply penalty quantum from one statute to another. The EPA prescribes five-year imprisonment for certain violations; WPA prescribes varying penalties. BD Act's Section 55 caps at three years — a moderate penalty that students may underestimate or overestimate by importing numbers from other Acts.
solution.final_explanation:
The BD Act uses a tiered penalty structure, and Section 55's specific quantum is a testable fact.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: One year is insufficient — Section 55 sets a higher ceiling to deter commercial biopiracy by Indian entities.
• Option (b) — Correct: Section 55 prescribes imprisonment up to three years, or a monetary fine, or both for contravening Section 7's intimation requirement. This applies to Indian citizens, companies, and organizations that access biological resources commercially without intimating the SBB.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Five years is the penalty prescribed under the Environment Protection Act, 1986 — not under Section 55 of the Biological Diversity Act.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Ten-year imprisonment is not prescribed in the BD Act for any offence.

Value Addition:
• The same Section 55 penalty applies to contraventions of Section 3 (foreign entity violations) — symmetrical penalty quantum across tiers.
• NBA has power to compound offences; SBBs must approach courts for enforcement — asymmetry in compounding authority.
• Section 61 requires a formal complaint by NBA or SBB before any court can take cognizance of Section 55 offences.

solution.concept_anchor: State Biodiversity Fund Section 32 — sources and permissible uses

statement_analysis.statement: The State Biodiversity Fund established under Section 32 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 may be used for conservation of biological diversity and for the socio-economic development of local communities living in or near areas rich in biological resources.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 32 explicitly permits these two uses — conservation of biodiversity and socio-economic development of local communities — as the primary permissible uses of the State Biodiversity Fund.

statement_analysis.statement: The State Biodiversity Fund receives contributions exclusively from Access and Benefit Sharing proceeds collected by State Biodiversity Boards from Indian companies accessing biological resources.
statement_analysis.reason: The State Biodiversity Fund's sources are not exclusively ABS proceeds — it is also funded by grants from the State Government, fees collected under the BD Act, and potentially contributions from the national fund channeled through the NBA. Stating ABS proceeds as the exclusive source is a partial-truth that omits other funding streams.

statement_analysis.statement: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India has no jurisdiction to audit the State Biodiversity Fund since it is not part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
statement_analysis.reason: CAG audit oversight applies to State Biodiversity Funds — CAG's jurisdiction extends to funds of statutory bodies and state-level funds receiving government grants, regardless of whether they are part of the Consolidated Fund of India.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who know Statement 2 is incorrect (ABS-exclusive source claim) may assume Statement 3 (CAG jurisdiction) is correct based on the Consolidated Fund reasoning, choosing only Statement 2 as the incorrect one.
elimination_logic: The question asks which statements are NOT correct — identify the false statements.
Statement 1: Conservation of biodiversity and socio-economic development of local communities as permissible uses — correctly stated; Statement 1 is correct (not incorrect).
Statement 2: 'Exclusively from ABS proceeds' — the fund has multiple sources including state grants and fees; the exclusivity claim is a partial-truth; Statement 2 is NOT correct.

Statement 3: CAG has no jurisdiction over State Biodiversity Fund — this is incorrect; CAG oversight extends to statutory funds including state biodiversity funds receiving government money; Statement 3 is NOT correct.
Statements 2 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a technically-sounding but erroneous argument — the 'Consolidated Fund' reasoning. Students who recall that CAG primarily audits the Consolidated Fund of India may accept that a separate state fund escapes CAG scrutiny. In practice, CAG's jurisdiction under the Comptroller and Auditor General's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971 extends to all bodies substantially funded by government grants — including statutory bodies like SBBs managing State Biodiversity Funds.
solution.final_explanation:
The State Biodiversity Fund's funding sources and audit oversight are precision points that test statutory knowledge beyond surface-level familiarity.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 32 authorizes use of the State Biodiversity Fund for conservation of biological diversity and socio-economic development of local communities — both are explicitly mentioned permissible purposes.
• Statement 2 — NOT correct: The State Biodiversity Fund is funded from multiple sources — fees under the BD Act, grants from State Government, ABS proceeds, and transfers from the NBA national fund. 'Exclusively ABS proceeds' overstates one source while excluding others.
• Statement 3 — NOT correct: CAG's audit jurisdiction is not limited to the Consolidated Fund of India. It extends to all statutory bodies and entities receiving government grants. State Biodiversity Funds managed by SBBs (which are statutory bodies) are subject to CAG audit oversight.

Value Addition:
• Section 27 (National Biodiversity Fund, managed by NBA) and Section 32 (State Biodiversity Fund, managed by SBBs) are parallel provisions — memorize both.
• CAG reports on SBBs have been a source of evidence for parliamentary committees flagging biodiversity governance gaps.
• Fund utilization transparency is a reform demand — digitization of SBB financial records is being advocated in governance reviews.

solution.concept_anchor: BHS notification — State Government, not SBB; dual notification possible

statement_analysis.statement: Under Section 37 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, the State Government notifies Biodiversity Heritage Sites in consultation with local bodies — the State Biodiversity Board plays an advisory role but is not the notifying authority.
statement_analysis.reason: Section 37 vests notification power in the State Government acting in consultation with local bodies. The SBB advises but does not issue the notification — a critical distinction that students frequently invert.

statement_analysis.statement: Once an area is notified as a Biodiversity Heritage Site under the BD Act, it cannot simultaneously be declared a Wildlife Sanctuary or National Park under the Wildlife Protection Act, 1972, as the two statutes operate under mutually exclusive legal regimes.
statement_analysis.reason: There is no legal bar to dual notification — a single area can be both a Biodiversity Heritage Site under the BD Act and a Wildlife Sanctuary or National Park under the Wildlife Protection Act. The two statutes operate under different legal frameworks but are not mutually exclusive in territorial application.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who correctly know Statement 1 and who assume environmental protection laws avoid territorial overlap may accept Statement 2 as also true, choosing (a).
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Section 37's notification power rests with State Government; SBB is advisory — correctly stated; Statement 1 is correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: Dual notification as both BHS and Wildlife Sanctuary is legally possible — no mutual exclusion exists; Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 1 correct, Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits students' intuition that overlapping legal regimes create conflicts requiring exclusion. In India's environmental law, overlapping protections are common — areas can simultaneously be Ramsar sites, National Parks, Tiger Reserves, and BHS. The BD Act does not contain any provision excluding BHS notification for areas already protected under WPA, and WPA does not exclude BHS notification either. Students who assume exclusivity without checking the statutory text will mark Statement 2 as correct.
solution.final_explanation:
Biodiversity Heritage Site notification and its relationship with other protection regimes is a nuanced governance point.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Section 37 is explicit — State Governments notify BHS areas in consultation with local bodies. The SBB's role is advisory in this process: it may recommend areas, provide scientific assessments, and facilitate consultation, but the notification authority vests in the State Government.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: India's environmental protection framework routinely creates overlapping protection designations. A single area may simultaneously carry Ramsar Wetland status, National Park status under WPA, and BHS status under the BD Act. There is no statutory provision in either the BD Act or the WPA creating mutual exclusion. Dual notification is legally possible and has precedent.

Value Addition:
• The management responsibility post-BHS notification typically rests with local bodies and State Government — SBBs remain in an advisory capacity even post-notification.
• BHS designation, unlike WPA Protected Area declaration, does not carry mandatory resettlement provisions — making it less contentious but also less protective.
• As of 2024, several states have multiple BHS notifications — Maharashtra, Kerala, and Karnataka are among the active notifying states.

solution.concept_anchor: BD Act broader than WPA — SBB covers agro-biodiversity and landraces
solution.strong_distractor: b — Students who correctly identify both A and R as true may assume the broad scope of the BD Act explains SBBs' agro-biodiversity mandate, but need to verify whether R specifically and causally explains A rather than being a parallel fact.
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? — Yes. SBBs' mandate under the BD Act extends to agro-biodiversity and landraces — the Act covers 'biological resources' broadly, not just wild species, and SBBs interface with the PPV&FR Act, 2001 on this.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? — Yes. The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 does take a Schedule-based approach focused on listed wild species — it does not cover cultivated varieties or agricultural biodiversity.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? — Yes. The reason SBBs have a broader mandate (including agro-biodiversity) is precisely because the BD Act's scope is wider than WPA's species-centric approach. R explains why A is the case — the BD Act's breadth versus WPA's narrowness directly explains why SBBs cover agro-biodiversity.
Both A and R are correct and R explains A — select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The scope distinction between the Biological Diversity Act and the Wildlife Protection Act is fundamental to understanding SBBs' mandate.

Assertion (A): Correct. SBBs' mandate under the BD Act covers biological resources broadly — including agro-biodiversity, landraces, and cultivated varieties. This is distinct from the WPA's species-centric, Schedule-based conservation approach. SBBs interface with the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 on agro-biodiversity matters.

Reason (R): Correct. The Wildlife Protection Act, 1972 operates through Schedules listing specific wild species for protection. It does not cover agricultural varieties, traditional crop varieties (landraces), or cultivated biological resources.

Causal Link: R genuinely explains A. The BD Act's broader scope (which R correctly describes as distinct from WPA's narrower approach) is the direct reason SBBs have jurisdiction over agro-biodiversity — they are implementing a statute that covers all biological resources, not just wild listed species.

Correct option: (a) — Both A and R correct, R explains A.

Value Addition:
• India is a mega-biodiversity hotspot with over 47,000 plant species — SBBs' broad mandate reflects this diversity.
• The PPV&FR Act, 2001 protects farmers' varieties and breeders' rights — SBBs and PPV&FRA Authority have complementary agro-biodiversity mandates.
• Marine cultivated species (aquaculture) in coastal states add another dimension to SBBs' agricultural biodiversity mandate.

solution.concept_anchor: 2023 Amendment exemptions — AYUSH, seed sector, codified TK, Indian researchers

statement_analysis.statement: The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 exempts AYUSH practitioners from BD Act compliance requirements including the prior intimation obligation to State Biodiversity Boards.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2023 Amendment explicitly exempts AYUSH practitioners from BD Act provisions.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2023 Amendment declares that seed varieties registered under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001 are exempt from the Biological Diversity Act's access and benefit-sharing provisions.
statement_analysis.reason: The seed sector exemption is a documented and controversial change in the 2023 Amendment reducing SBBs' ABS oversight over the commercial seed industry.

statement_analysis.statement: The 2023 Amendment extends the exemption for codified traditional knowledge to all forms of traditional knowledge, including knowledge that is undocumented and held only in community oral tradition.
statement_analysis.reason: The exemption is limited to 'codified' traditional knowledge — systematically documented in classical texts. Undocumented oral knowledge remains within the BD Act's ambit.

statement_analysis.statement: Foreign nationals and foreign-incorporated companies remain subject to the National Biodiversity Authority's prior approval requirements even after the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023.
statement_analysis.reason: The 2023 Amendment's exemptions targeted domestic actors; foreign entity requirements under Section 3 and NBA approval remain unchanged.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Students who correctly identify Statements 1, 2, and 4 as correct may over-extend Statement 3's 'codified TK' exemption to all traditional knowledge, marking all four correct and choosing (d).
elimination_logic: Statement 1: AYUSH practitioners' exemption under 2023 Amendment — documented and correct.
Statement 2: Seed sector/PPV&FR registered varieties exempt from ABS provisions — correctly stated.

Statement 3: Extension of exemption to undocumented oral traditional knowledge — the 2023 Amendment specifies 'codified' knowledge only; undocumented oral knowledge is not covered by this exemption; Statement 3 is incorrect.
Statement 4: Foreign entity NBA approval requirements unchanged by 2023 Amendment — correctly stated.
Three statements (1, 2, 4) are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 uses a scope-extension technique — extending 'codified traditional knowledge' to 'all traditional knowledge including oral.' The 2023 Amendment's critics and biodiversity experts specifically flagged that the exemption's limitation to codified knowledge creates a two-tier system. Students who broadly know 'traditional knowledge is exempted' without the codified/uncodified distinction will mark Statement 3 as correct, incorrectly inflating the count to four.
solution.final_explanation:
The 2023 Amendment introduced significant exemptions that reduce SBBs' regulatory load but also weaken ABS oversight.

solution.concept_anchor: No formal joint inspection mechanism — NBA-SBB implementation gap
solution.strong_distractor: a — Students who know the BD Act has strong inter-tier linkages (Section 23(d) implementing NBA guidelines, fund flows) may assume a joint inspection mechanism must also exist — it sounds institutionally logical.
elimination_logic: The question asks which describes an acknowledged gap in NBA-SBB institutional coordination.
Eliminate (a): A Joint Biodiversity Inspection Commission sounds authoritative but does not exist under the BD Act — plausible fabrication.
Eliminate (c): Annual report submission by SBBs to State Legislatures and NBA to Parliament exists and is accurate — this is NOT a gap but an existing mechanism.
Eliminate (d): Fund flow from NBA to SBBs exists in the BD Act framework — not a gap.

Select (b): No formal joint inspection or monitoring mechanism between NBA and SBBs is prescribed in the BD Act — this is a well-documented implementation gap acknowledged in biodiversity governance reviews.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is a plausible-fabrication trap. 'Joint Biodiversity Inspection Commission' does not exist, but it sounds like exactly the kind of body the BD Act should have created. Students who reason institutionally — 'a three-tier structure must have joint inspection mechanisms' — will mark (a) as a real mechanism rather than a fabricated one. The question tests whether students know the absence of such a mechanism is precisely the governance gap being examined.
solution.final_explanation:

This is an acknowledged governance gap — the two tiers share data informally and implement guidelines under Section 23(d) but have no prescribed protocol for joint field operations or monitoring.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Annual reporting exists and functions — SBBs report to State Legislatures and NBA reports to Parliament. This is a strength, not a gap.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: ABS proceeds are channeled from NBA's national fund to SBBs for state-level conservation — the financial linkage exists, not a gap.
